sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: White Cubes was a site-specific installation that took shape on the interconnected rooftops of Yazd's historical neighbourhood.

By reviving white mosquito nets, as a construct that was part of the summer and nightlife rhythm for the locals during her childhood, Fazael Ardakani brought a collective experience to a new level and raised new questions about the private space of mosquito nets.
The project was formed by installing fifteen mosquito nets, borrowed from the neighbors.

The mosquito nets that once defined the ambiguous boundary between private and public on the roofs of Yazd: Spaces that the locals used as sleeping quarters and a place to spend their nightlife, and while being private, they had no distinct boundary, as they were almost visible to every spectator.
This time, the same dual quality was revived: A private space situated within a collective space.
The audience would sit inside the mosquito nets, pray, rest, experience an intimate atmosphere, converse, or just relax for a moment.
The project was not a visual object, but a "situation"; a platform to simultaneously experience closeness, memory, and presence.

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: The connected rooftops of the houses in Yazd were not only an architectural setting but also a part of the past collective life of the city. The project was executed in this very space at the invitation of Persbook 8 Festival, a space that is simultaneously private and public, and provided the possibility of a direct experience of the urban fabric and lived traditions.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: Relying on the simplicity of form and the cultural weight of the material, the installation posed a contemporary question: How can a possibility for participation, dialogue, and confrontation with the city be created from an everyday element? How do private and public boundaries shift in urban life? Can collective memory be activated by summoning a familiar element? How does participation occur when it is not prescribed? For the artist, distancing herself from galleries based on the art economy and seeking other forms of connection with the audience and social participation was also a part of the motivation.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: The main tension of the project was the institutional reaction to a photo capturing �a kiss�, inside one of the mosquito nets. When this photo was shared on social media by the artist and some other artists, a member of the Persbook team requested its removal and to make sure it wouldn�t be displayed on any platform. Later, the same photo was published in a book, but at the artist's request, without direct reference to the name "Persbook" and in a modified format, so that both the work could be preserved and further confrontations could be avoided.

sections.title: About the Artist
paragraphs: Bio: Fatemeh Fazael Ardakani is an artist who lives and works between Tehran and Ardakan. This constant commuting between two distinct spaces has shaped her perspective on the notion of space and time. She has turned the boundaries between the personal world and collective questions into the main arena of her artistic work, creating projects that are not born in the studio, but in the context of real life and interstitial spaces.

In her works, she utilizes familiar and culturally loaded materials. For her, incorporating these materials is not merely an artistic medium but an intermediary for creating a dialogue with history and society. In her works, the audience is not just a spectator, but an active partner in the creation of meaning. By creating situations where the audience plays an active role � through entering the space, touching, and even tasting parts of the artwork � Fazael Ardakani emphasizes the importance of this direct and unmediated participation. For her, each project is a response to the question of how one can both live and think critically in a world full of contradictions. Her work is a continuous search, not for offering definitive answers, but for raising better and more meaningful questions.
Instagram: @fatemeh.fazayel
Website: www.fatemehfazayel.com

According to the artist, each individual chose a specific form of participation based on their needs or mood; sometimes someone would enter the mosquito net to pray, a group of friends would go there to talk and rest, a couple had a close and intimate experience, like kissing in that space, and shared this moment in conversation with the artist. Even some tourists or the artists themselves chose the mosquito net as a place to relax and rest.

For the artist, creating communication models based on lived experience and collective memory has been important: �First, it was the revival of a shared memory through a familiar element like a mosquito net. This old element itself was a communication medium that, without the need for words, invited people to converse and recall shared memories. Second, creating a multi-functional space that gave the audience freedom of action. I deliberately did not predetermine exactly how people should interact with the work. Thus, I witnessed everyone using the space according to their personal needs, from praying to friendly conversations and even intimate experiences.�

Third, blurring the boundary between private and public space, which also existed in the vernacular architecture of Yazd. Old mosquito nets had exactly this characteristic - they were both a private and a public space. This feature allowed people to be present in a collective space while maintaining privacy. Fourth, involving the community in the creation of the work from the very beginning. �When I borrowed the mosquito nets from the neighbors, I inadvertently involved them in the process of creating the work.� This took the work out of the artist's monopoly and turned it into a collective project. And finally, creating a direct dialogue with the urban fabric that separates the project from the gallery space. �This was a response to my personal concern to break out of the commercial frameworks of art and create a more vital connection with the audience. In fact, instead of creating a purely visual object, I created a 'situation' where people played an active role. Art in this project was not a commodity, but a platform for shared experience."
